newsitem.title: USA: Too early to gauge quality of Texas HRW wheat.
newsitem.headline: Too early to gauge quality of Texas HRW wheat.

text.p: The ongoing delay in harvesting the Texas hard red winter wheat crop means that it is still too early to assess overall quality characteristics, grain merchandisers said on Monday.

"Basically, we're running about two weeks behind average harvest (pace) because of the cool, damp weather that we've had across our state," said Rodney Mosier, executive assistant of Texas Wheat Producers.
The weather has hindered the crop's ability to mature and has also kept farmers from working in fields.
Mosier said there had been some spot cutting around Fort Worth and Wichita Falls, but he cautioned against reading too much into the characteristics of those samples.
"It's not an overall indicator of the whole Texas crop," Mosier said. "Probably in another six or seven days we'll know what's going on."
One merchandiser in Fort Worth said that his firm had received between 15 and 20 truckloads of wheat Monday morning.
"It's a little early to measure, but the first load we dumped was all number one wheat. I haven't seen any of the other numbers like protein content or anything," he said.

Another merchandiser in south central Kansas said he had heard reports of protein content in the Texas crop ranging "on every end of the spectrum." He said reports of protein content had been as low as 10 percent and as high as 15.5 percent.
Wheat industry sources said that just as it was still too early to get an idea of the Texas crop quality, it was equally difficult to estimate crop yields.
A trader at the Kansas City Board of Trade said his contacts in Corpus Christi, Texas, had been reluctant to furnish any yield estimates because of the delay in harvesting the crop.

Mosier said despite delaying harvest activities, the cool, wet spring was a net positive phenomenon because it allowed secondary wheat tillers to develop and in many cases replace primary tillers that were damaged or destroyed by a freeze that hit the Plains in mid-April.
"We couldn't have asked for a better blessing than to have cool, wet weather help our crop along after the freeze damage," Mosier said.
